lessons.title: Data Cleaning: Handling Missing Values
lessons.body: Missing data is common in African datasets. For example, a mobile money dataset from Kenya might have missing transaction amounts because of network issues. If you ignore missing values, your AI model will make wrong predictions. First, identify missing values using Python's pandas: `df.isnull().sum()`. Then decide how to handle them. If less than 5% of a column is missing, you can drop those rows: `df.dropna(subset=['amount'], inplace=True)`. But dropping too many rows loses valuable data. For numerical columns, fill missing values with the mean or median. In a Nigerian agricultural dataset with missing crop yields, use the median because it's robust to outliers: `df['yield'].fillna(df['yield'].median(), inplace=True)`. For categorical columns, fill with the most frequent value (mode): `df['region'].fillna(df['region'].mode()[0], inplace=True)`. Better yet, use predictive imputation: train a simple model to predict missing values based on other columns. For time-series data like daily sales in a Ghanaian market, use forward-fill: `df['sales'].fillna(method='ffill', inplace=True)`. Always document your imputation method and check if it introduces bias. Tools: pandas, scikit-learn's SimpleImputer. Remember, cleaning data is 80% of the work. Start with a plan: explore, quantify, then choose a method. In Africa, where data collection can be inconsistent, robust imputation is key to reliable AI.

lessons.title: Data Normalization and Standardization
lessons.body: When features have different scales, AI models like K-Nearest Neighbors or neural networks perform poorly. For instance, in a dataset of African businesses, 'annual revenue' might range from 10,000 to 10,000,000 USD, while 'number of employees' ranges from 1 to 500. Without scaling, revenue dominates distance calculations. Normalization (min-max scaling) rescales features to a 0-1 range: `X_norm = (X - X_min) / (X_max - X_min)`. Use scikit-learn's MinMaxScaler: `from sklearn.preprocessing import MinMaxScaler; scaler = MinMaxScaler(); X_scaled = scaler.fit_transform(X)`. This is good when you need bounded values, like for image pixels. Standardization (Z-score) transforms data to have mean 0 and standard deviation 1: `X_std = (X - mean) / std`. Use StandardScaler: `from sklearn.preprocessing import StandardScaler; scaler = StandardScaler(); X_scaled = scaler.fit_transform(X)`. This is better for algorithms that assume Gaussian distribution, like linear regression or PCA. For African datasets with outliers (e.g., a few very large transactions), standardization is more robust. Always fit the scaler on training data only, then transform test data to avoid data leakage. In practice, use pipelines: `from sklearn.pipeline import Pipeline; pipe = Pipeline([('scaler', StandardScaler()), ('model', LogisticRegression())])`. This ensures consistent scaling. Remember, scaling doesn't change the shape of the distribution, just the range. Test both methods and see which improves your model's accuracy.

lessons.title: Categorical Encoding Techniques
lessons.body: Most AI models require numerical input, so categorical data like 'country' or 'product category' must be encoded. For nominal categories (no order), use one-hot encoding. In a dataset of African countries, 'country' has values like 'Kenya', 'Nigeria', 'Ghana'. One-hot creates binary columns: `pd.get_dummies(df, columns=['country'])`. This works well for low-cardinality features (less than 10 categories). But if you have 50 categories, it creates 50 columns, causing the curse of dimensionality. For high-cardinality, use label encoding: assign each category a unique integer: `from sklearn.preprocessing import LabelEncoder; le = LabelEncoder(); df['country_encoded'] = le.fit_transform(df['country'])`. But label encoding implies order, which may mislead models. For ordinal categories (with order), like 'education level' (Primary, Secondary, Tertiary), use ordinal encoding: map to 1,2,3. For advanced cases, use target encoding: replace category with the mean target value. In a Nigerian loan dataset, encode 'city' by the average loan default rate. But beware of overfitting; use cross-validation. Another technique is binary encoding, which uses fewer columns. Tools: category_encoders library. Always handle unseen categories in test data: use `handle_unknown='ignore'` in OneHotEncoder. In Africa, where categorical features like 'mobile network' are common, choose encoding based on model type and cardinality. Tree-based models can handle label encoding, but linear models need one-hot.

lessons.title: Feature Scaling and Transformation
lessons.body: Beyond basic scaling, feature transformation can make your data more normal and improve model performance. For skewed data, like income in many African countries where a few people earn much more, apply a log transformation: `df['income_log'] = np.log1p(df['income'])`. This reduces skewness and makes patterns more linear. For counts data, like number of daily transactions, use square root or Box-Cox transformation. Box-Cox finds the best power transformation: `from scipy.stats import boxcox; df['transformed'], _ = boxcox(df['count'] + 1)`. For features with outliers, use robust scaling: `from sklearn.preprocessing import RobustScaler; scaler = RobustScaler(); X_scaled = scaler.fit_transform(X)`. This uses median and interquartile range, so outliers don't dominate. Another technique is discretization (binning): convert continuous features into categories. For age, create bins: 'young', 'middle', 'old'. Use `pd.cut(df['age'], bins=[0, 25, 50, 100], labels=['young', 'middle', 'old'])`. This can help linear models capture non-linear relationships. For text data, use TF-IDF or word embeddings. In African context, transforming features like 'distance to nearest market' can reveal patterns. Always visualize before and after: use histograms and Q-Q plots. Remember, transformation should be based on training data and applied to test data. Use pipelines to automate. Experiment with different transformations and evaluate with cross-validation. The goal is to make your data more suitable for the model, not to perfect the distribution.

lessons.title: Feature Selection Methods
lessons.body: Not all features are useful; some add noise and slow down training. Feature selection picks the most relevant ones. Start with filter methods: calculate correlation between each feature and target. In a dataset predicting crop yield in Tanzania, features like 'rainfall' and 'fertilizer' might have high correlation, while 'farmer's name' has none. Use `df.corr()['yield'].sort_values(ascending=False)`. For categorical, use chi-square test: `from sklearn.feature_selection import chi2; chi2_scores, p_values = chi2(X, y)`. Select features with p-value < 0.05. Wrapper methods like Recursive Feature Elimination (RFE) train a model and remove weakest features iteratively: `from sklearn.feature_selection import RFE; selector = RFE(estimator=LogisticRegression(), n_features_to_select=5); selector.fit(X, y)`. Embedded methods like Lasso (L1 regularization) shrink coefficients to zero: `from sklearn.linear_model import Lasso; lasso = Lasso(alpha=0.1); lasso.fit(X, y); selected = X.columns[lasso.coef_ != 0]`. For tree-based models, use feature_importances_: `from sklearn.ensemble import RandomForestClassifier; rf = RandomForestClassifier(); rf.fit(X, y); importances = rf.feature_importances_`. In Africa, where data collection is expensive, feature selection reduces cost and improves interpretability. Always use cross-validation to avoid overfitting. Start with domain knowledge: include features that make sense. Then use automated methods. A smaller set of good features often beats a large set of mediocre ones.

lessons.title: Dimensionality Reduction with PCA
lessons.body: When you have many features (e.g., 100 columns from survey data), dimensionality reduction simplifies the data while preserving important information. Principal Component Analysis (PCA) is the most common technique. It creates new features (principal components) that are linear combinations of original features, capturing maximum variance. For example, in a dataset of African households with 50 variables, PCA might reduce to 10 components that explain 95% of variance. Steps: standardize data first (PCA is sensitive to scale). Then: `from sklearn.decomposition import PCA; pca = PCA(n_components=0.95); X_pca = pca.fit_transform(X_scaled)`. This keeps components that explain 95% variance. You can also specify number: `pca = PCA(n_components=10)`. Check explained variance ratio: `pca.explained_variance_ratio_`. Use scree plot to decide number of components. PCA helps with visualization: reduce to 2D or 3D and plot. It also speeds up training and reduces overfitting. But PCA components are less interpretable; you lose original feature meanings. For interpretability, use feature selection instead. In Africa, PCA is useful for high-dimensional data like satellite imagery or genomic data. Apply PCA after handling missing values and encoding categoricals. Always fit PCA on training data only. For non-linear data, use Kernel PCA or t-SNE. Remember, PCA assumes linear relationships; if data is highly non-linear, consider autoencoders. Start with PCA as a baseline, then try other methods.

lessons.title: Practical Reference
lessons.body:
Practical Reference: Data Preprocessing and Feature Engineering for African Agribusiness

In African agribusiness, data rarely arrives clean. A maize cooperative in Ghana may log yields in WhatsApp messages, a Kenyan dairy processor might track milk volumes in handwritten ledgers, and a Nigerian poultry farm could record feed consumption across three different spreadsheets with inconsistent units. Before any AI model can forecast demand, detect disease, or optimize logistics, the data must be cleaned, transformed, and reduced to the features that actually drive decisions.

This practical reference consolidates the six lessons in this module into a working checklist for African agribusiness teams. It assumes you have already collected data from field agents, mobile money platforms, IoT sensors, or satellite imagery. The goal is simple: turn messy operational data into a reliable feature set that a model can learn from â without losing the business context that makes African agriculture unique.

Data Cleaning: Handling Missing Values

Missing data in African agribusiness is rarely random. A farmer may not report yield because the harvest failed, a sensor may go offline during the rainy season, or a mobile money transaction may be missing because the network was down. Before imputing, ask why the value is missing. If missingness itself carries business meaning â for example, a missing loan repayment could signal default risk â create a binary indicator feature instead of simply filling the gap.

For numerical features like rainfall, temperature, or yield per hectare, median imputation is often safer than mean imputation because agricultural data frequently has outliers from exceptional harvests or droughts. For categorical features like crop type or region, use the most frequent category or a dedicated "Unknown" category. When missingness exceeds 40â50% in a column, consider dropping the feature entirely unless it is business-critical.

Table 1: Missing Value Strategies for Common Agribusiness Features
Feature Typical Missing % Recommended Strategy Business Rationale
Yield (kg/ha) 15â30% Median imputation by region and season Preserves local agronomic context
Rainfall (mm) 5â20% Interpolation from nearest weather station Rainfall is spatially correlated
Crop type 10â25% Mode imputation or "Unknown" category Maintains categorical integrity
Mobile money transactions 20â40% Forward fill + missing indicator Missingness may signal financial stress
GPS coordinates 30â50% Impute from village centroid Enables spatial clustering

Source: Adapted from FAO (2022), "Agricultural Data Governance" and GIZ (2021), "Data-Driven Agriculture in Africa."

Data Normalization and Standardization

African agribusiness datasets often mix scales: farm size in hectares (0.5â50), annual revenue in USD (500â500,000), and rainfall in millimeters (200â2,000). Models that rely on distance calculations â k-nearest neighbors, support vector machines, and PCA â will be dominated by the largest-scale feature unless you normalize or standardize.

Use min-max normalization when you need values bounded between 0 and 1, such as for neural networks. Use z-score standardization when your data has outliers or when the algorithm assumes a Gaussian distribution. For seasonal data like monthly milk production, consider seasonal decomposition before scaling so that the underlying trend is not distorted.

Table 2: Scaling Methods Compared for Agribusiness Features
Method Formula Best For African Ag Example
Min-Max Normalization (x â min) / (max â min) Neural networks, bounded inputs Normalizing soil pH to 0â1
Z-Score Standardization (x â mean) / std PCA, SVM, linear models Standardizing rainfall across regions
Robust Scaling (x â median) / IQR Data with outliers Farm revenue with extreme values
Log Transformation log(x + 1) Skewed distributions Mobile money transaction amounts

Source: Adapted from Scikit-learn preprocessing documentation (Pedregosa et al., 2011) and World Bank (2020), "Digital Agriculture in Sub-Saharan Africa."

Categorical Encoding Techniques

Categorical variables are everywhere in African agribusiness: crop type (maize, cassava, sorghum), region (Ashanti, Oromia, Kano), season (long rains, short rains, dry), and market channel (cooperative, broker, direct). One-hot encoding works well for low-cardinality features (fewer than 10 categories). For high-cardinality features like district or cooperative name, use target encoding or frequency encoding to avoid exploding the feature space.

Be careful with ordinal categories. A feature like "farm size category" (small, medium, large) has a natural order and should be encoded as 0, 1, 2 rather than one-hot. For cyclical features like month or day of week, use sine and cosine transformations to preserve the cyclical relationship â critical for modeling planting and harvest cycles.

Feature Scaling and Transformation

Beyond basic scaling, African agribusiness data often benefits from transformations that capture domain knowledge. Yield per hectare is more meaningful than total yield when comparing farms of different sizes. Rainfall deviation from the seasonal average is more predictive than raw rainfall. Price ratios between maize and fertilizer can reveal farmer profitability better than either price alone.

Create interaction features that reflect real business relationships: rainfall Ã fertilizer application, or distance to market Ã transport cost. These engineered features often outperform raw variables in predictive models because they encode the agronomic and economic logic that domain experts already know.

Feature Selection Methods

More features do not always mean better models. In African agribusiness, where data collection is expensive and noisy, feature selection improves both accuracy and interpretability. Use filter methods (correlation, mutual information) for a quick first pass. Use wrapper methods (recursive feature elimination) when you have enough data and compute. Use embedded methods (LASSO, tree-based importance) when you want selection to happen during model training.

Always validate feature selection with local experts. A feature that looks statistically weak â such as distance to the nearest paved road â may be critical for logistics planning even if it does not improve yield prediction. Business value and statistical significance are not the same thing.

Dimensionality Reduction with PCA

Principal Component Analysis (PCA) is particularly useful for African agribusiness when working with satellite imagery, which can have dozens or hundreds of spectral bands. PCA reduces these bands into a few components that capture most of the variance, making models faster and less prone to overfitting.

However, PCA has a critical limitation: the resulting components are linear combinations of original features and are often difficult to interpret. If your business stakeholders need to understand which factors drive a prediction â for example, to explain a loan decision to a farmer â PCA may not be the right choice. Use it for preprocessing satellite or sensor data, but prefer interpretable feature selection for decision-facing models.

â ï¸ Safety Warning: Do Not Leak Future Information

When preprocessing time-series agribusiness data â such as monthly yields, rainfall, or prices â always fit your imputation, scaling, and PCA transformations on the training set only, then apply them to the test set. Fitting on the full dataset causes data leakage and produces models that look accurate in testing but fail in the field. This is especially dangerous in crop yield forecasting, where a leaked future rainfall value can make a model appear highly accurate while being useless for real planting decisions. Always split your data chronologically, not randomly, for agricultural time series.

Quick Reference Checklist

  1. Understand missingness before imputing. Ask why data is missing â it may carry business meaning. Create missing indicators where relevant.
  2. Choose imputation by feature type. Median for skewed numerical data, mode or "Unknown" for categorical, interpolation for spatially correlated weather data.
  3. Match scaling to the algorithm. Min-max for neural networks, z-score for PCA and SVM, robust scaling when outliers are present.
  4. Encode categoricals thoughtfully. One-hot for low cardinality, target or frequency encoding for high cardinality, ordinal encoding for ordered categories.
  5. Engineer domain-driven features. Yield per hectare, rainfall deviation, price ratios, and interaction terms often outperform raw variables.
  6. Select features with business input. Combine statistical methods with agronomist and operations team review before finalizing the feature set.
  7. Use PCA for high-dimensional sensor and satellite data, but prefer interpretable features for decision-facing models.
  8. Prevent data leakage. Fit all transformations on training data only, and split time-series data chronologically.

Further Reading

  • Scikit-learn: Preprocessing Data â Official documentation on scaling, normalization, and encoding.
  • FAO: Agricultural Data Governance and Use â Free FAO publication on data quality in agriculture.
  • World Bank: Digital Agriculture in Africa â Reports on data-driven agribusiness across Sub-Saharan Africa.
  • Google: Data Preparation and Feature Engineering â Free course material on preprocessing pipelines.
  • Kaggle: Feature Engineering â Free hands-on course covering encoding, scaling, and selection.

This practical reference is part of the Rise AFRICA Skills AI Fundamentals course. For agribusiness teams, the goal is not perfect data â it is data that is clean enough, scaled appropriately, and reduced to the features that drive real decisions on the farm, in the cooperative, and along the value chain.

quiz.q: What is the first step when handling missing values in a dataset?
options: A) Drop all rows with missing values
B) Identify and quantify missing values
C) Fill missing values with zeros
quiz.explanation: You must first identify where and how many missing values exist before deciding on a strategy.

quiz.q: Which method is best for filling missing numerical values when outliers are present?
quiz.explanation: Median is robust to outliers, unlike the mean which can be skewed by extreme values.

quiz.q: What does the pandas method `df.isnull().sum()` do?
options: B) Counts missing values per column
D) Replaces missing values with mean
quiz.explanation: It returns the number of missing values in each column.

quiz.q: For time-series data, which imputation method is often used?
quiz.explanation: Forward-fill carries the last observed value forward, which is suitable for time-series.

quiz.q: What is the main difference between normalization and standardization?
options: A) Normalization scales to 0-1, standardization to mean 0 and std 1
B) Normalization uses mean, standardization uses median
C) Normalization is for categorical, standardization for numerical
quiz.explanation: Normalization (min-max) bounds values to [0,1]; standardization (Z-score) centers to mean 0 and scales to unit variance.

quiz.q: Which scaler is more robust to outliers?
quiz.explanation: RobustScaler uses median and interquartile range, making it less sensitive to outliers.

quiz.q: Why should you fit a scaler only on training data?
quiz.explanation: Fitting on training data only prevents information from the test set from influencing the scaling, avoiding data leakage.

quiz.q: What is the purpose of a pipeline in scikit-learn?
options: B) To chain preprocessing and modeling steps
quiz.explanation: A pipeline sequentially applies a list of transforms and a final estimator, ensuring consistent preprocessing.

quiz.q: Which encoding technique is best for nominal categorical variables with low cardinality?
quiz.explanation: One-hot encoding creates binary columns for each category without implying order, ideal for low-cardinality nominal data.

quiz.q: What is a disadvantage of one-hot encoding for high-cardinality features?
options: B) It creates too many columns
quiz.explanation: High cardinality leads to a large number of binary columns, causing dimensionality issues.

quiz.q: Which encoding method is suitable for ordinal categories?
quiz.explanation: Ordinal encoding assigns integers based on the order of categories, preserving the ranking.

quiz.q: What is target encoding?
options: A) Encoding based on the target variable
D) Encoding based on binary representation
quiz.explanation: Target encoding replaces a category with the mean of the target variable for that category.

quiz.q: Which library provides advanced categorical encoding techniques?
quiz.explanation: The category_encoders library offers many encoding methods like target encoding, binary encoding, etc.

quiz.q: When should you use label encoding?
options: A) For nominal data with many categories
B) For ordinal data or tree-based models
quiz.explanation: Label encoding is suitable for ordinal data and can be used with tree-based models that can handle integer splits.

quiz.q: What does a log transformation do to skewed data?
quiz.explanation: Log transformation compresses the range of large values, reducing right skewness.

quiz.q: Which transformation is best for count data?
quiz.explanation: Log, square root, and Box-Cox are all suitable for count data depending on the distribution.

quiz.q: What is the purpose of discretization?
options: A) To convert continuous features to categorical
B) To convert categorical to continuous
quiz.explanation: Discretization (binning) transforms continuous variables into discrete intervals.

quiz.q: Which of the following is a robust scaling method?
quiz.explanation: RobustScaler uses statistics that are robust to outliers, such as median and IQR.

quiz.q: What is the main goal of feature selection?
options: A) To increase the number of features
B) To select the most relevant features
quiz.explanation: Feature selection aims to identify and keep the most useful features for the model.

quiz.q: Which filter method uses correlation?
quiz.explanation: All these are filter methods; Pearson correlation is for numerical features, chi-square for categorical.

quiz.q: What does RFE stand for?
quiz.explanation: RFE is a wrapper method that recursively removes less important features.

quiz.q: Which regularization method can perform feature selection?
quiz.explanation: L1 regularization (Lasso) and Elastic Net (which combines L1 and L2) can shrink coefficients to zero, effectively selecting features.

quiz.q: How can you get feature importances from a Random Forest?
quiz.explanation: Random Forest models have a feature_importances_ attribute that indicates the importance of each feature.

quiz.q: What is the curse of dimensionality?
options: A) Too many features make models perform worse
B) Too few features make models perform worse
quiz.explanation: As the number of features increases, the data becomes sparse, making it harder for models to learn patterns.

quiz.q: What does PCA stand for?
quiz.explanation: PCA is a dimensionality reduction technique that finds principal components.

quiz.q: What should you do before applying PCA?
quiz.explanation: PCA is sensitive to scale, so standardizing the data is recommended.

quiz.q: How do you decide the number of components in PCA?
quiz.explanation: All these methods help determine the optimal number of components.

quiz.q: What is a disadvantage of PCA?
options: D) It cannot handle large datasets
quiz.explanation: Principal components are linear combinations of original features, making them harder to interpret.

quiz.q: When is PCA most useful?
options: A) When features are highly correlated
quiz.explanation: PCA is effective when features are correlated, as it combines them into components capturing shared variance.

quiz.q: What is the difference between PCA and feature selection?
options: A) PCA creates new features, feature selection keeps original
B) PCA keeps original features, feature selection creates new
quiz.explanation: PCA transforms data into new components, while feature selection retains a subset of original features.
